analysis.one_liner: Sets pay rules and protections for college athletes and lets schools pool TV rights under antitrust protection.
analysis.headline: Introduced on June 4, 2026 and referred to three House committees, the bill has sat untouched since — no hearing, no vote, no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill turns the terms of the court settlement in the college athlete NIL litigation into permanent law: schools and their boosters can pay athletes only up to a shared revenue cap, and that cap continues indefinitely with inflation adjustments. In exchange for accepting that ceiling, athletes get a package of protections — a guarantee they can sign name, image, and likeness deals, required medical coverage including five years of injury costs after they stop playing, scholarship protection from being revoked for injury or performance, one penalty-free transfer, and the right to sue abusive agents. The bill also gives schools and conferences a limited antitrust exemption to pool and sell their television rights, requiring at least 75% of big-football schools to join.
analysis.who_benefits: Division I college athletes gain the most concrete protections: guaranteed access to NIL deals, required coverage of out-of-pocket injury costs during and for five years after playing, catastrophic injury insurance, a ban on revoking scholarships for injury, poor performance, or roster cuts, one free transfer, an ombudsman office, athlete seats on governing boards, and the right to sue agents who defraud them, with no forced arbitration. Schools and conferences also gain, by getting a permanent, court-proof cap on what they must pay athletes and antitrust immunity to sell media rights as a bloc.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Division I college athletes and schools

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits schools, conferences, and the NCAA from restricting student athletes from earning NIL compensation or entering NIL agreements, subject to limited exceptions like unauthorized use of school trademarks.

Requires institutions to cover out-of-pocket medical costs for sports injuries during participation and for five years after an athlete's last competition, plus catastrophic injury insurance above $90,000 and a $60 million association fund for long-term conditions like chronic traumatic encephalopathy.
Bars institutions from revoking, reducing, or conditioning an athlete's scholarship based on athletic performance, injury or illness, or roster-management decisions.
Lets athletes transfer once without losing eligibility, and transfer freely in additional circumstances such as a coach's departure, discontinued sport, or sexual assault or harassment.

Requires athlete agents to register with a state, caps endorsement-contract fees at 5%, voids noncompliant contracts at the athlete's option, and gives athletes a private right of action with pre-dispute arbitration agreements unenforceable.

Requires at least one-third of intercollegiate athletic association governing boards to be current or former student athletes, and establishes an Office of the Student Athlete Ombudsman with retaliation protection.
Requires comparable standards for medical care, lodging, meals, and facilities across similarly situated men's and women's programs.

analysis.who_pays: Star athletes and the booster collectives that currently pay them above the settlement cap pay the most: the bill makes the cap permanent and forbids schools, their employees, and any entity acting for a school from arranging compensation that circumvents it. Big-spending athletic departments bear new medical coverage, reporting, and compliance costs. If the pooled media-rights exemption is used, broadcasters and fans could face a less competitive rights market, though the bill also requires market-level broadcast access for football and basketball games.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes the House settlement's revenue share cap permanent, with annual inflation adjustments, so athletes' total pay from schools and their boosters stays capped even after the court settlement expires or is terminated.

It prohibits institutions, conferences, and any associated entity — including collectives and donors who have given over $50,000 to a school — from arranging compensation that would circumvent the cap, cutting off the uncapped collective payments star athletes currently receive.

It grants a limited antitrust exemption for institutions and conferences that form joint agreements to sell sports telecasting rights, requiring participation from at least 75% of Football Bowl Subdivision schools, which could concentrate broadcasting rights in fewer hands.

The antitrust exemption also covers enforcement of the pay cap, the eligibility and transfer rules, and recruitment and tampering restrictions, shielding those rules from antitrust challenge so long as the association implements them.
The bill declares neutrality on whether student athletes are employees, leaving unresolved the question of whether athletes could unionize or bargain collectively.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The athlete protections are real and unusually concrete for a sports bill: guaranteed medical coverage after playing careers end, scholarships that survive injury, and enforceable rights against agents and schools. But the price is written into the same text — a permanent ceiling on athlete pay and antitrust immunity for the schools' media-rights cartel. For most athletes, who earn little or nothing from NIL today, the protections likely outweigh the cap. For star football and basketball players, the cap forecloses uncapped collective payments that are currently legal, which is a substantial loss. The overall design is a bargain struck between athlete protection and institutional control, and it leans toward institutional control by making the cap permanent rather than leaving it to expire with the settlement.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced and has not moved since; with Congress still in session, it has simply been sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Baumgartner introduced the bill in the House on June 4, 2026.
It was referred the same day to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Workforce Committees.
No hearing, markup, vote, or other action has been recorded since the referral.
The 119th Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027, so the bill is not yet dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained: the NCAA and member schools keep operating under the court-approved settlement unchanged, and athletes' current rights are unchanged. The schools avoid any new medical, transparency, or governance obligations for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — schools keep status quo

for.name: Rep. Michael Baumgartner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Workforce.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans appear in the record — one sponsor and one cosponsor — and no Democrat, no committee action, and no floor vote has shown where the parties stand.

industries.note: The bill locks the settlement's pay cap into permanent law and grants antitrust immunity for enforcing it and for pooling media rights, cementing the associations' control over college sports economics. At the same time it imposes medical coverage, transparency, ombudsman, and athlete-representation requirements on them, so they are regulated even as their core powers are entrenched.

Collectives are barred from arranging compensation that circumvents the revenue cap and are swept into the bill's definitions of associated entities subject to penalties. Because the money they move goes directly to athletes, restricting them also restricts what athletes can earn above the cap.

Schools gain a permanent pay ceiling on athletes and antitrust immunity for media-rights pooling, which helps control costs. They also take on new medical coverage, scholarship protection, reporting, and health-and-safety obligations, whose interests in cost control run against athlete pay.

An antitrust-exempt pooled sale of Football Bowl Subdivision telecasting rights could consolidate rights in fewer hands, while a new market-level broadcast access requirement for football and basketball could make more games available to local viewers.

Agents must register with a state, face a 5% fee cap on endorsement contracts, and can be sued and decertified for violations. Athletes gain a private right of action and cannot be forced into pre-dispute arbitration over agent disputes.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor and no committee action in the months since its June 2026 referral, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027; bills referred to three committees with no recorded support typically die at the end of a Congress.
